interviewQuestions.question: What's the actual difference between a star schema and a snowflake schema, and which would you default to?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
They're the same fact-and-dimension idea, differing only in how far the dimensions are normalized. Star keeps every dimension flat — a product dimension carries category name and brand name as plain columns. Snowflake normalizes those further into their own sub-dimension tables, so getting a brand name means an extra join or two through the product-to-category-to-brand chain.

I'd default to star on a modern columnar warehouse, and here's the reasoning rather than just the answer: dictionary encoding makes repeated text nearly free to store, while joins are a real, scaling cost on a distributed engine, especially once a fact table is in the billions of rows. Snowflaking trades a near-zero cost for a real one, which is the wrong trade most of the time.

I wouldn't say never snowflake, though — a genuinely huge, slowly-changing, widely-shared sub-dimension can still earn a normalized table. I'd treat it as a per-dimension call backed by size and update-frequency numbers, not a schema-wide policy.

**Testing:** whether you understand the trade-off's mechanics well enough to default correctly and still know the exception.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: A teammate wants to normalize the product dimension into product, category, and brand tables because it's "cleaner." How do you respond?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd separate the aesthetic argument from the cost argument, because "cleaner" is doing a lot of unexamined work in that sentence. Normalization avoids duplicate data — that's a real value in OLTP, where inconsistent writes are the actual risk. A dimension table isn't written to constantly and isn't at risk of write inconsistency, so the benefit normalization is meant to deliver mostly doesn't apply here.

What normalizing this dimension *does* cost is concrete: every report that touches product category or brand — which, realistically, is most of them — now pays two extra joins, forever, on every run. The storage it saves is close to a rounding error once dictionary encoding compresses the repeated category and brand names.

So my response would be to ask for the actual numbers: how big is the category/brand data, how often does it change, how many queries touch it? If those don't justify the join cost, I'd keep it flat and say so directly — "cleaner" isn't a reason on its own when the concrete cost is paid by every future query and the benefit is nearly zero here.

**Testing:** whether you can push back on an aesthetic argument with a concrete cost-benefit case instead of deferring to "best practice."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: Give me a real case where snowflaking a dimension is the right call, not just a textbook exercise.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The case that holds up is a dimension that's genuinely large, changes on its own schedule, and is reused across many other dimensions or fact tables — geography is the cleanest example. A `dim_geography` with country, region, city, and postal-code detail can be a meaningfully large table on its own, and if a dozen other dimensions (customer, store, shipping address) all reference the same geography hierarchy, keeping it as one normalized, shared table means an admin boundary change — a city getting reassigned to a new region — updates in one place instead of fanning out across every dimension that had flattened a copy.

A second real case: when a sub-dimension is owned by a different team as its own product, like a shared product taxonomy maintained centrally. Normalizing it isn't really a storage decision there — it's an ownership boundary, and a separate table is the natural expression of that.

What I'd avoid citing as a justification is "it might grow large someday" — that's speculative and doesn't earn the join cost today. The real cases are ones where the size, update pattern, or ownership boundary already exists, not a hypothetical future one.

**Testing:** whether you can name a concrete, defensible exception instead of treating star-vs-snowflake as an absolute rule either way.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Applied judgement

interviewQuestions.question: You inherit a warehouse where every dimension is fully snowflaked. Reports are slow and analysts complain the SQL is hard to write. What would you do?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I wouldn't rip out the whole schema on day one — I'd start by measuring where the join cost is actually concentrated, since "every dimension is snowflaked" doesn't mean every dimension deserves it. I'd look at query logs for the most-run reports and see how many joins each one pays and how much of total query time is join-bound versus scan-bound.

From there, I'd flatten the highest-traffic, lowest-justification dimensions first — the ones with no strong size or update-frequency case for staying normalized, that show up in the most dashboards. That's the highest-leverage fix: fewer joins on the queries that run thousands of times a day, with the least risk since you're only touching dimensions where the case for snowflaking was weak anyway.

I'd leave alone any sub-dimension that has a real justification — genuinely huge, or centrally owned by another team — and document why, so the next person doesn't "fix" it back into a flattening mistake. I'd frame this to stakeholders as an incremental migration with measured wins at each step, not a rewrite, since a full re-model of a live warehouse carries real risk of breaking existing reports.

**Testing:** whether you can prioritize a schema remediation by actual query cost rather than treating it as an all-or-nothing rewrite.
